description: We are Year 1 Aerospace Engineering students working on the Lunar Landing Site Navigation challenge.
summary: We developed an interactive Lunar Landing Site Navigator designed to help assess the suitability of potential landing sites on the Moon. Users can either enter geographical coordinates manually or select from a range of pre-defined locations, including but not limited to historical Apollo landing sites and Chandrayaan missions. The application analyses the selected location using lunar elevation data and astronomical calculations to evaluate environmental conditions over a specified period. It generates graphs showing solar and Earth elevation, visibility periods and the lunar horizon at different times. Additionally, image processing techniques are used to identify potential impact basins and craters surrounding the selected location. The project aims to bring together geographical data, astronomical modelling and image analysis in one accessible interface, helping users understand the environmental conditions and potential challenges associated with lunar landing site selection.
details: It plots a point on a 2D rendition of the Moon's surface taking the longitude and latitude as input. This can be done by manually entering it or by selecting a site from the dropdown menu. The program then generates 3 figures. The first figure showcases the sun and earth elevation, the green highlighted zone being the time where both are within suitable limits. It also displays the elevation data by querying the LOLA dataset which contains information on the moon's elevation. The second figure uses machine imaging to locate dar spots and basins near that point using OpenCV's CV2. The third figure uses the time slider to showcase the position of the sun and the earth relative to the horizon of the moon during the time period which can be input. The project is intended to allow both researchers and educators to showcase the data required for planning a moon mission in a digestible yet informative way. This project was coded entirely in python, notably using tkinter for the GUI, astropy for querying the JPL Horizon's database and rasterio to query the LOLA dataset without loading all 8GB into memory. Our project showcases creativity using the horizon view which is a visual plot of the Earth and Sun's locations relative to the horizon at that point on the moon. We considered the Earth and Sun's elevation and azimuth, the time period, the longitude, latitude and elevation of the point on the surface of the moon, and machine imaging of nearby basins.
